raw_text:
{{RunningHeader|thin|6291|thing}}and deriv.), also ταναός (for *ταναϝος; in comp. ταναυ-), stretched out, slim, long, thin, taper, = Skt. ''tanu'', stretched out, thin; orig. ‘stretched out,’ connected with a verb seen in AS. *''thenian'', *''thennan'', in comp. ''ā-thenian'' = OHG. ''dennan'', MHG. ''denen'', G. ''dehnen'' = Goth. *''thanjan'', in comp. ''uf-thanjan'', stretch out (a secondary form of AS. *''thenan'', etc.), = L. ''tendere'', stretch (''tenere'', hold), = Gr. τείνειν, stretch, = Skt. √ ''tan'', stretch, etc. A very prolific root; from the L. adj. are ult. E. ''tenuous'', ''tenuity'', ''attenuate'', ''extenuate'', etc., and from the L. verb root are ult. E. ''tend''1, ''attend'', ''intend'', etc., ''tendon'', etc. (see ''tend''1); from the Gr., ''tone'', ''tonic'', etc., ''tænia'', ''tasis'', etc.] 1. Very narrow in all diameters; slender; slim; long and fine: as, a ''thin'' wire; a ''thin'' string. {{smaller block|Then the priest shall see the plague; and, behold, if . . . there be in it a yellow ''thin'' hair, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean. {{right|Lev. xiii. 30.}}}} {{smaller block|Comes the blind Fury with the abhorred shears, And slits the ''thin''-spun life. {{right|''Milton'', Lycidas, l. 76.}}}} 2. Very narrow in one diameter; having the opposite surfaces very near together; having little thickness or depth; not thick; not heavy: as, ''thin'' paper; ''thin'' boards: opposed to ''thick''. {{smaller block|Kerue not thy brede to ''thynne'', Ne breke hit not on twynne. {{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 18.}}}} {{smaller block|I'm a cold; this white satin is too ''thin'' unless it be cut, for then the sun enters. {{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, iv. 4.}}}} {{smaller block|The Judge had put on his ''thinnest'' shoes, for the birch-bark canoe has a delicate floor. {{right|''C. F. Woolson'', Jupiter Lights, xv.}}}} '''3.''' Having the constituent parts loose or sparse in arrangement; lacking density, compactness, or luxuriance; rare; specifically, of the air and other gases, rarefied. {{smaller block|The men han ''thynne'' Berdes and fewe Heres; but thei ben longe. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 207.}}}} {{smaller block|These our actors, As I foretold you, were all spirits, and Are melted into air, into ''thin'' air. {{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iv. 1. 150.}}}} {{smaller block|And woods, made ''thin'' with winds, their scatter'd honours mourn. {{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Horace's Odes, I. xxix. 64.}}}} '''4.''' Hence, easily seen through; transparent, literally or figuratively; shallow; flimsy; slight: as, a ''thin'' disguise. {{smaller block|I come not To hear such flattery now, and in my presence; They are too ''thin'' and bare to hide offences. {{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., v. 3. 125.}}}} {{smaller block|Throned in the centre of his ''thin'' designs, Proud of a vast extent of flimsy lines! {{right|''Pope'', Prol. to Satires, l. 93.}}}} {{smaller block|We bear our shades about us; self-depriv'd Of other screen, the ''thin'' umbrella spread. {{right|''Cowper'', Task, i. 260.}}}} '''5.''' Having slight consistency or viscosity: said of liquids: as, ''thin'' syrup; ''thin'' gruel.—'''6.''' Deficient in some characteristic or important ingredient; lacking strength or richness; specifically, of liquors, small: opposed to ''strong''. {{smaller block|I couthe selle Bothe dregges and draf, and draw at one hole Thicke ale and ''thynne'' ale. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xxii. 402.}}}} {{smaller block|If I had a thousand sons, the first humane principle I would teach them should be to forswear ''thin'' potations. {{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iv. 3. 134.}}}} {{smaller block|When banes are craz'd, an' bluid is ''thin.'' {{right|''Burns'', First Epistle to Davie.}}}} '''7.''' Of sound, lacking in fullness; faint, and often somewhat shrill or metallic in tone. {{smaller block|''Thin'' hollow sounds, and lamentable screams. ''Dryden.''}} {{smaller block|In a clear voice and ''thin'' The holy man 'gan to set forth the faith. {{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, II. 287.}}}} '''8.''' Limited in power or capacity; feeble; weak. {{smaller block|My tale is doon, for my wytte is ''thynne.'' {{right|''Chaucer'', Merchant's Tale, l. 438.}}}} {{smaller block|On the altar a ''thin'' flickering flame Just showed the golden letters of her name. {{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 384.}}}} '''9.''' Meager; lean; spare; not plump or fat. {{smaller block|And the seven ''thin'' ears devoured the seven rank and full ears. {{right|Gen. xli. 7.}}}} {{smaller block|No meagre, muse-rid mope, adust and ''thin'', In a dun night-gown of his own loose skin. {{right|''Pope'', Dunciad, ii. 37.}}}} {{smaller block|His face is growing sharp and ''thin.'' {{right|''Tennyson'', Death of the Old Year.}}}} '''10.''' Limited in quantity or number; small or infrequent; scanty. {{smaller block|You are like to have a ''thin'' and slender pittance. {{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., iv. 4. 61.}}}} {{smaller block|The ''thin'' remains of Troy's afflicted host In distant realms may seats unenvied find. {{right|''Addison'', tr. of Horace's Odes, iii. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|Mr. Powell has a very full congregation, while we have a very ''thin'' house. {{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 14.}}}} 11. Scantily occupied or furnished; bare; empty: used absolutely or with ''of''. {{smaller block|The cheerfulness of a spirit that is blessed will make a ''thin'' table become a delicacy. {{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Holy Living, ii. 6.}}}} {{smaller block|The University being ''thin'' this Vacation time, the contributions designed for me go on but slowly. {{right|''Rev. Simon Ockley'' (Ellis's Lit. Letters, p. 353).}}}} {{smaller block|When a nation abounds in physicians, it grows ''thin of'' people. {{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 21.}}}} 12. Having no depth: said of a school of fish. —13. Having insufficient density or contrast to give a good photographic print or a satisfactory image on the screen; weak: said of a negative or a lantern-slide.—'''Thin register.''' {{smaller|See ''register''1, 5 (''b'').—'''Through thick and thin.''' See ''thick''.—'''Too thin,''' failing to convince; easily seen through; not sufficient to impose on one.}} '''thin1''' (thin), ''adv.'' [< ''thin''1, ''a.''] Thinly. {{smaller block|Ere you come to Edinburgh port, I trow ''thin'' guarded sall ye be. {{right|''Sang of the Outlaw Murray'' (Child's Ballads, VI. 35).}}}} '''thin1''' (thin), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''thinned'', ppr. ''thinning''. [< ME. ''thynnen'', < AS. ''ge-thynnan'', make thin, < ''thynne'', thin: see ''thin''1, ''a.''] I. ''trans.'' To make thin. {{smaller|(''a'') To attenuate; draw or spread out thin; hence, to reduce in thickness or depth: as, to ''thin'' a board by planing.}} {{smaller block|How the blood lies upon her cheek, all spread As ''thinned'' by kisses! {{right|''Browning'', Pauline.}}}} {{smaller|(''b'') To make less dense or compact; make sparse; specifically, to rarefy, as a gas.}} {{smaller block|Who with the ploughshare clove the barren moors, . . . ''Thinned'' the rank woods. {{right|''Wordsworth'', Off Saint Bees' Heads.}}}} (''c'') To reduce in consistency or viscosity: said of liquids: as, to ''thin'' starch. (''d'') To reduce in strength or richness: as, to ''thin'' the blood. (''e'') To make lean or spare. {{smaller block|A troublous touch
''Thinn'd'' or would seem to ''thin'' her in a day. {{right|''Tennyson'', Aylmer's Field.}}}} (''f'') To reduce in numbers or frequency. {{smaller block|One half of the noble families had been ''thinned'' by proscription. {{right|''Hallam'', Middle Ages, iii. 8.}}}} {{smaller block|Many a wasting plague, and nameless crime,
And bloody war that ''thinned'' the human race. {{right|''Bryant'', Death of Slavery.}}}} (''g'') To make bare or empty. {{smaller block|The oppressive, sturdy, man-destroying villains . . .
''Thin'd'' states of half their people. ''Blair'', The Grave.}} {{smaller block|For attempting to keep up the fervor of devotion for so long a time, we have ''thinned'' our churches. {{right|''Sydney Smith'', in Lady Holland, iii.}}}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become thin. (''a'') To diminish in thickness; grow or become thin: with ''out'', ''away'', etc.: thus geological strata are said to ''thin out'' when they gradually diminish in thickness till they disappear. (''b'') To become less dense, compact, or crowded; become sparse; hence, to become scattered; separate. {{smaller block|The crowd in Rotten Row begins to ''thin.'' {{right|''Bulwer'', My Novel, v. 4.}}}} {{smaller block|My hair is ''thinning'' away at the crown,
And the silver fights with the worn-out brown. {{right|''W. S. Gilbert'', Haunted.}}}} '''thin'''2†, ''pron.'' A Middle English form of ''thine.'' '''thine''' (ᴛ̵ʜīn), ''pron.'' [In defs. 1 and 2 orig. gen. of ''thou''; < ME. ''thin'', ''thyn'', < AS. ''thīn'' (= OS. OFries. ''thīn'' = OHG. MHG. ''dīn'', G. ''dein'', ''deiner'' = Icel. ''thīn'' = Goth. ''theina''), gen. of ''thū'', thou: see ''thou.'' In def. 3 merely poss. (adj.), < ME. ''thin, thyn,'' < AS. ''thīn'' = OS. ''thīn'' = OFries. ''thīn, din'' = MD. ''dijn'' = OHG. MHG. ''dīn,'' G. ''dein'' = Icel. ''thīnn, thīn, thītt'' = Sw. Dan. ''dīn'' = Goth. ''theins,'' thine; poss. adj. Hence, by loss of the final consonant, ''thy.'' For the forms and uses, cf. ''mine''1.] 1†. Of thee; the original genitive of the pronoun ''thou.'' {{smaller block|To-mo[r]we ye sholen ben weddeth, And, maugre ''thin,'' to-gidere beddeth. {{right|''Havelok'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1127.}}}} 2. Of thee; belonging to thee. Compare ''mine''1, 2. {{smaller block|Ich haue for-gyue the meny gultes and my grace graunted Bothe to the and to ''thyne'' in hope thow sholdest a-mende. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), iv. 135.}}}} {{smaller block|O, if to fight for king and commonweal Were piety in ''thine,'' it is in these. {{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., i. 1. 115.}}}} 3. Belonging or pertaining to thee: in this sense a possessive. {{smaller|(''a'') Used predicatively.}} {{smaller block|"Mi sone," heo sede, "haue this ring, Whil he is ''thin'' ne dute nothing That fur the brenne, ne adrenche se." {{right|''King Horn'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 51.}}}} {{smaller block|A drope of blode if atte thou tine We gif ȝou dome, the wrange is ''thine.'' {{right|''Holy Rood'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 111.}}}} {{smaller block|''Thine'' is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. {{right|Mat. vi. 13.}}}} {{smaller block|"Take thou my robe," she said, "for all is ''thine.''" {{right|''Tennyson'', Holy Grail.}}}} {{smaller|(''b'') Used attributively, with the force of an adjective: commonly preferred before a vowel to ''thy,'' and now used only in that situation.}} {{smaller block|Alle ''thine'' castles Ich habbe wel istored. {{right|''Layamon'', l. 13412.}}}} {{smaller block|Sythen alle ''thyn'' other lymeȝ lapped ful clene, Thenne may thou se thy sauior & his sete ryche. {{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), ii. 175.}}}} {{smaller block|Drink to me only with ''thine'' eyes. {{right|''B. Jonson'', To Celia.}}}} '''Mine and thine''', a phrase noting the division of property among different owners, and implying the right of individual ownership; meum and tuum. {{smaller block|Amonge them [Cubans] the lande is as common as the sonne and water; And that ''Myne and Thyne'' (the seedes of all myscheefe) haue no place with them. {{right|''Peter Martyr'' (tr. in Eden's First Books on America, ed. [Arber, p. 78).}}}} {{smaller|[''Thine'', like ''thou'', is now used only in poetry, in solemn discourse, always in prayer, provincially in England, and in the common language of the Friends. In familiar and common language ''your'' and ''yours'' are always used in the singular number as well as the plural.]}} '''thing1''' (thing), ''n.'' [< ME. ''thing'', ''thyng'', < AS. ''thing'', sometimes ''thincg'', ''thinc'', a thing, also a cause, sake, office, reason, council, = OS. OFries. ''thing'' = D. ''ding'' = OHG. ''dinc'', MHG. ''dinc'', G. ''ding'' = Icel. ''thing'', a thing (rare), pl. articles, objects, things, valuables, jewels, also an assembly, meeting, parish, district, county, shire, parliament, = Sw. Dan. ''ting'' = Goth. *''thigg'' (not recorded); cf. AS. deriv. ''thingian'', make an agreement, contract, settle, compose (a quarrel), speak, = G. ''dingen'', hold court, negotiate, make a contract (''bedingen'', make conditions, stipulate); prob. related to Goth. ''theihs'' (for *''thinhs''?), time, L. ''tempus'', time: see ''tense''1, ''temporal''1. For the development of sense, cf. AS. ''sacu'' (= G. ''sache'', etc.), contention, strife, suit, cause, case, thing (see ''sake''1); also L. ''res'', a cause, case, thing, L. ''causa'', a cause, case, ML. and Rom. (It. ''cosa'' = F. ''chose''), a thing. The sense ‘a concrete inanimate object’ is popularly regarded as the fundamental one, but a general notion such as that could hardly be original.] 1. That which is or may become the object of thought; that which has existence, or is conceived or imagined as having existence; any object, substance, attribute, idea, fact, circumstance, event, etc. A thing may be either material or ideal, animate or inanimate, actual, possible, or imaginary. {{smaller block|Thei gon gladly to Cypre, to reste hem on the Lond, or elles to bye ''thingis'' that thei have nede to here lyvynge. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 29.}}}} {{smaller block|We were as glad of day lyght as euer we were of any ''thynge'' in all our lyues. {{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 73.}}}} {{smaller block|Scripture indeed teacheth ''things'' above nature, ''things'' which our reason by itself could not reach unto. {{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, iii. 8.}}}} {{smaller block|Consider not the ''things'' of this life, which is a very prison to all God's children, but the ''things'' of everlasting life, which is our very home. {{right|''J. Bradford'', Letters (Parker Soc., 1853), II. 64.}}}} {{smaller block|So prevalent a ''Thing'' is Custom that there is no altering of a Fashion that has once obtain'd. {{right|''N. Bailey'', tr. of Colloquies of Erasmus, I. 371.}}}} {{smaller block|He [Pepys] must always be doing something agreeable, and, by way of preference, two agreeable ''things'' at once. {{right|''R. L. Stevenson'', Men and Books, p. 290.}}}} {{smaller block|In more limited applications—(''a'') A particular existence or appearance which is not or cannot be more definitely characterized; a somewhat; a something.}} {{smaller block|What, has this ''thing'' appear'd again to-night? {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 1. 21.}}}} {{smaller block|A ''thing'' which Adam had been posed to name; Noah had refused it lodging in his ark. {{right|''Pope'', Satires of Donne, iv. 25.}}}} {{smaller block|The round ''thing'' upon the floor is a table upon which the dishes of their frugal meal were set. {{right|''R. Curzon'', Monast. in the Levant, p. 84.}}}} (''b'') A living being: applied to persons or animals, either in admiration, tenderness, or pity, or in contempt: as, a poor sick ''thing''; a poor foolish ''thing''. {{smaller block|For Floriz was so fair ȝongling And Blauncheflur so suete ''thing''. {{right|''King Horn'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 71.}}}} {{smaller block|''Thing'' of talk, begone! Begone, without reply. {{right|''Ford'', Broken Heart, ii. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|The poor ''thing'' sighed, and, with a blessing, . . . turned from me. {{right|''Addison.''}}}} {{smaller block|The seeming-injured simple-hearted ''thing'' Came to her old perch back. {{right|''Tennyson'', Merlin and Vivien.}}}} (''c'') A material object lacking life and consciousness. {{smaller block|He himself Moved haunting people, ''things'', and places. {{right|''Tennyson'', Enoch Arden.}}}} {{smaller block|''Things'' differing in temperature, colour, taste, and smell agree in resisting compression, in filling space. Because of this quality we regard the wind as a ''thing'', though it has neither shape nor colour, while a shadow, though it has both but not resistance, is the very type of nothingness. {{right|''J. Ward'', Encyc. Brit., XX. 57.}}}} (''d'') That which is done; an act, doing, undertaking, business, affair, etc.; also, something which is to be done; a duty or task; in the passage from Chaucer, below, in the plural, prayers or devotions.
